title: Inside the growing vigilante movement to knock out Flock surveillance cameras
excerpt: An underground network of privacy activists is disabling or destroying the ubiquitous surveillance devices sprouting up across the US
content_html:
The first time that “NoMark” tried to knock out a Flock camera feed, he waited an hour for the perfect moment – pacing in and out of bushes that towered over him, a few feet behind a pole holding up the device.

“I was just so nervous,” he said.

NoMark, as he’s known on Instagram, had already gained an online following of hundreds of thousands for posting videos of himself wearing a black mask and taking on small-time vigilante missions: breaking up fights outside a bar and breaking into a refinery he believed was “polluting the city real bad”. The Minnesota Star Tribune dubbed him “Minneapolis’ Batman”. He spoke to the Guardian under condition of anonymity to discuss potentially illegal acts.

On this June night, he set his sights on a new target: automated license plate readers (ALPRs) made by the US company Flock Safety.

These black cameras, which are hooked up to a rectangular solar panel and typically mounted on a pole, snap photos of passing vehicles and run the pictures against large databases. They have sparked nationwide backlash from pro-privacy critics, who point to public records suggesting that these devices can help law enforcement keep tabs on specific license plates and the people driving these cars. That they can sweep in so many people’s location from an innocent act in a public space – regardless of whether the target is a suspect in a crime, and without a warrant – has led to fears of mass surveillance.

Flock, based in Georgia and valued at $8.4bn, says its cameras scan license plates billions of times each month in about 6,000 communities in nearly every state in the US.

The company said in a February blogpost that its ALPRs are “not mass surveillance tools” and that it “cannot track vehicles, much less individual people”.

Across the street from a Taco Bell, NoMark couldn’t stop thinking about whether he would get caught, and the adrenaline felt paralyzing – even though this felt “on brand” for his online persona, which has won him more than 700,000 followers on Instagram and TikTok. After a few minutes of not spotting any cars on the road, he climbed a few feet up the pole, taped up the camera to block its lens and snipped the wires that powered the whole operation. Then he ended his phone’s recording and fled.

Nowadays, NoMark is much calmer on these excursions, and it only takes him a few minutes to get the job done after having taken down more than a dozen cameras, he says. But he still assumes the police are looking for him. Even if he does get arrested, he’s hopeful the charges won’t be too severe – and more important, he “just wants to send a message”.

“I’m not afraid to do things if I think they’re right,” he says. “These things are coming up so fast across the country that this is kind of the only way to combat them.”

The Minneapolis camera destroyer is not alone. As anger grows towards law enforcement contracts with Flock, vigilantes across the country are taking matters into their own hands by smashing, obstructing or taking down these cameras. Many are leaning into their creative side: “paint bombing” the devices, planting American flags at the scene after damaging them, 3D printing objects to help obstruct the camera’s view and leaving colorful messages like “hahaha get wrecked ya surveilling fucks”. Some influencers are even creating fake cease-and-desist letters from Flock, capitalizing on the company’s negative public perception.

The Guardian has identified at least 33 instances of people damaging, vandalizing and destroying Flock cameras, across 23 states, that appear to have the explicit message of protesting surveillance.

Flock, along with police departments across the US, say these cameras are integral for public safety, and capture vehicle details that can help in investigations, such as license plate numbers and the make and model of vehicles. Flock’s website also advertises how these cameras can “stop crime in real time” by alerting officers “the moment a suspect car passes by” – suggesting that cops can act quickly on these leads to pursue a target. The company’s CEO, Garrett Langley, has described some pro-privacy critics as wanting to “normalize lawlessness” and “weaken public safety”.

NoMark has not been caught in his campaign against Flock cameras. Others are facing charges. Jeffrey Sovern in Suffolk, Virginia, has been charged with destruction of property for allegedly damaging more than a dozen Flock cameras. Sovern has not admitted to the act but did tell police that he finds these cameras to be unconstitutional.

He wrote on a GoFundMe created to pay for legal expenses: “I will take the silver lining that this can be a catalyst in a bigger movement to roll back intrusive surveillance.”

A handful of other cases have drawn criminal charges, too. In New Mexico, Jevon Martinez was arrested after allegedly destroying 13 Flock cameras.

When asked if he would “continue to take down these Flock cameras”, Martinez told local news station KRQE: “Absolutely. They are a clear and present threat to public safety.” The news outlet also reported that a sign near one of the damaged Flock cameras read: “You’re welcome, the Republic of New Mexico.”

Flock did not comment on vigilantes knocking out its cameras but did publish a blogpost in mid-July about helping government agencies respond if a camera is damaged.

“We’ve planned for it,” the company wrote, adding that protection plans are available for purchase.

Law enforcement is aware of the backlash and responding. Dozens of state fusion centers – collaborative hubs where federal and local agencies share intelligence about crime and terrorism – circulated memos across law enforcement agencies this summer directing officers to monitor anti-Flock advocacy as part of a directive to protect national security, according to reporting from journalist Dan Boguslaw. One report Boguslaw obtained from a Wisconsin intelligence agency calls for increased vigilance and patrols during protests and events such as a “national week of action” in mid-August. That intelligence digest also advised local law enforcement to report “vandalism, disruption or sabotage” of ALPRs to fusion centers.

Flock faces public blowback

The winds of sympathy online are not blowing in Flock’s favor. News articles and videos about vigilantes’ cases have drawn support from online commenters, who post made-up, neighborly alibis like seeing accused parties rescuing dogs or serving meals at a soup kitchen at the time a camera was destroyed.

The anti-Flock online ecosystem also features an exchange of tips and strategies for kneecapping the cameras. One Reddit poster shared a 3D print file for an object he says can help block cameras without damaging them or violating vandalism laws.

NoMark, in Minneapolis, says he receives dozens of messages daily from people wanting to help, letting him know they’re taking similar actions or asking for advice on staying safe. He keeps his replies vague, as he doesn’t want his words to get people arrested. He tells those writing to him to avoid driving past the cameras, and to make sure they’re going out late at night when they no one else is around. He reiterates that they should cover up completely, including their face and hands.

He also tells them: “Always cover the camera.”

Minneapolis’s Batman thinks you need both political pressure on elected officials and vigilantism to achieve change. He believes showing up to city council meetings – and he’s shown up to a few without his mask – is helpful but “it does obviously take time, and it’s not always effective”.

“The more time you take, the more data they get on people,” he said.

Privacy advocates pursue policy changes as vigilantes tear down cameras

More than 80 cities have disbanded, decided not to renew or rejected contracts with Flock in recent years, or deactivated the company’s cameras, including Austin and Denver, although activists remain concerned about the devices’ continued use in those areas.

Beyond general surveillance creep, privacy advocates fear US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s ability to access these camera feeds through legal loopholes to pursue immigrants.

Police officers have used the cameras for their own personal ends as well. Several have lost their jobs after misusing the devices to stalk people. Though license plate reading is the cameras’ bread and butter, 404 Media reported last week that cops have used Flock’s search feature to look for people with distinct markers – like tattoos and specific T-shirts – and not just cars.

Congress is taking note, and earlier this month a Texas lawmaker introduced a bill requiring warrants for data collected by Flock cameras.

Not all anti-Flock activism takes the form of camera destruction. A crowdsourced map created by the grassroots group DeFlock maps out more than 115,000 ALPRs across the country. The organization’s site also allows users to see if their license plates have been searched in Flock’s system, get directions to avoid ALPRs and find upcoming meetings about municipal Flock contracts.

Flock’s CEO has taken note of DeFlock’s advocacy, too, and characterized the organization as “terroristic” but recently apologized for that label. In a tweet, he attributed DeFlock’s popularity to his company’s “inadequate response to the questions and concerns that people have about ALPR”. The company is adapting to the backlash, canceling an always-on recording feature, “human distress detection”, which was intended to detect screaming.

A local chapter of DeFlock, in Norfolk, Virginia, says it does not endorse vigilantes targeting Flock cameras but does not advocate against it, either.

The Virginia chapter is working to ensure the city either cancels or does not renew its contract with Flock, but so far it hasn’t had success, and members are particularly angry about speaking restrictions on the topic. At a city council meeting last month, the mayor enforced a rule about reducing repetitive comments to limit the number of speakers who wanted to share their concerns about Flock, the Virginian-Pilot reported.

“We recognize it’s the inevitable outcome of a system designed to prevent people’s voices from being heard,” said a DeFlock spokesperson.

sentences.zh: 随着人们对与 Flock 签订的执法合同越来越愤怒，全国各地的治安维护者开始自行动手，砸碎、阻碍或拆除这些摄像机。

sentences.en: Many are leaning into their creative side: “paint bombing” the devices, planting American flags at the scene after damaging them, 3D printing objects to help obstruct the camera’s view and leaving colorful messages like “hahaha get wrecked ya surveilling fucks”.
sentences.zh: 许多人都在发挥自己的创意：对设备进行“油漆轰炸”，在损坏设备后在现场插上美国国旗，3D 打印物体来帮助遮挡摄像机的视线，并留下诸如“哈哈哈，你们这群监控者都被毁了”之类的彩色信息。

sentences.en: Some influencers are even creating fake cease-and-desist letters from Flock, capitalizing on the company’s negative public perception.
sentences.zh: 一些有影响力的人甚至利用公众对该公司的负面看法，伪造 Flock 的停止函。

blocks.html_en: The Guardian has identified at least 33 instances of people damaging, vandalizing and destroying Flock cameras, across 23 states, that appear to have the explicit message of protesting surveillance.

blocks.html_en: Flock, along with police departments across the US, say these cameras are integral for public safety, and capture vehicle details that can help in investigations, such as license plate numbers and the make and model of vehicles. Flock’s website also advertises how these cameras can “stop crime in real time” by alerting officers “the moment a suspect car passes by” – suggesting that cops can act quickly on these leads to pursue a target. The company’s CEO, Garrett Langley, has described some pro-privacy critics as wanting to “normalize lawlessness” and “weaken public safety”.

sentences.en: Flock, along with police departments across the US, say these cameras are integral for public safety, and capture vehicle details that can help in investigations, such as license plate numbers and the make and model of vehicles.
sentences.zh: 弗洛克和美国各地的警察部门表示，这些摄像头对于公共安全来说是不可或缺的，它们可以捕捉有助于调查的车辆详细信息，例如车牌号码以及车辆的品牌和型号。

sentences.en: Flock’s website also advertises how these cameras can “stop crime in real time” by alerting officers “the moment a suspect car passes by” – suggesting that cops can act quickly on these leads to pursue a target.
sentences.zh: 弗洛克的网站还宣传这些摄像头如何通过“可疑车辆经过时”向警察发出警报来“实时制止犯罪”，这表明警察可以根据这些线索迅速采取行动追捕目标。

sentences.en: The company’s CEO, Garrett Langley, has described some pro-privacy critics as wanting to “normalize lawlessness” and “weaken public safety”.
sentences.zh: 该公司首席执行官加勒特·兰利 (Garrett Langley) 表示，一些支持隐私的批评者希望“使无法无天的行为正常化”并“削弱公共安全”。

Sovern has not admitted to the act but did tell police that he finds these cameras to be unconstitutional.

sentences.en: Others are facing charges.

sentences.en: Flock did not comment on vigilantes knocking out its cameras but did publish a blogpost in mid-July about helping government agencies respond if a camera is damaged.

blocks.html_en: Law enforcement is aware of the backlash and responding. Dozens of state fusion centers – collaborative hubs where federal and local agencies share intelligence about crime and terrorism – circulated memos across law enforcement agencies this summer directing officers to monitor anti-Flock advocacy as part of a directive to protect national security, according to reporting from journalist Dan Boguslaw. One report Boguslaw obtained from a Wisconsin intelligence agency calls for increased vigilance and patrols during protests and events such as a “national week of action” in mid-August. That intelligence digest also advised local law enforcement to report “vandalism, disruption or sabotage” of ALPRs to fusion centers.

sentences.en: Law enforcement is aware of the backlash and responding.
sentences.zh: 执法部门意识到了这种强烈反对并做出了回应。

sentences.en: Dozens of state fusion centers – collaborative hubs where federal and local agencies share intelligence about crime and terrorism – circulated memos across law enforcement agencies this summer directing officers to monitor anti-Flock advocacy as part of a directive to protect national security, according to reporting from journalist Dan Boguslaw.
sentences.zh: 据记者 Dan Boguslaw 报道，数十个州融合中心——联邦和地方机构共享犯罪和恐怖主义情报的协作中心——今年夏天在执法机构之间分发了备忘录，指示官员监控反 Flock 的宣传，作为保护国家安全指令的一部分。

sentences.zh: 博古斯瓦夫从威斯康星州情报机构获得的一份报告呼吁在抗议活动和八月中旬的“全国行动周”等活动期间提高警惕和巡逻。

sentences.zh: 该情报摘要还建议当地执法部门向融合中心报告对 ALPR 的“破坏、破坏或破坏”行为。

blocks.html_en: The winds of sympathy online are not blowing in Flock’s favor. News articles and videos about vigilantes’ cases have drawn support from online commenters, who post made-up, neighborly alibis like seeing accused parties rescuing dogs or serving meals at a soup kitchen at the time a camera was destroyed.

sentences.en: The winds of sympathy online are not blowing in Flock’s favor.

sentences.zh: 有关治安维持者案件的新闻文章和视频得到了网上评论者的支持，他们发布了捏造的、睦邻不在场的证据，比如在相机被毁时看到被告方营救狗或在施粥厨房提供食物。

blocks.html_en: NoMark, in Minneapolis, says he receives dozens of messages daily from people wanting to help, letting him know they’re taking similar actions or asking for advice on staying safe. He tells those writing to him to avoid driving past the cameras, and to make sure they’re going out late at night when they no one else is around. He reiterates that they should cover up completely, including their face and hands.

blocks.html_en: More than 80 cities have disbanded, decided not to renew or rejected contracts with Flock in recent years, or deactivated the company’s cameras, including Austin and Denver, although activists remain concerned about the devices’ continued use in those areas.

sentences.en: More than 80 cities have disbanded, decided not to renew or rejected contracts with Flock in recent years, or deactivated the company’s cameras, including Austin and Denver, although activists remain concerned about the devices’ continued use in those areas.

blocks.html_en: Beyond general surveillance creep, privacy advocates fear US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s ability to access these camera feeds through legal loopholes to pursue immigrants.

sentences.en: The Virginia chapter is working to ensure the city either cancels or does not renew its contract with Flock, but so far it hasn’t had success, and members are particularly angry about speaking restrictions on the topic.

content_html_zh:
“NoMark”第一次尝试破坏 Flock 摄像机的信号时，他等了一个小时才等到完美的时刻——在高耸于他上方的灌木丛中踱来踱去，距离支撑设备的杆子后面几英尺。

“我只是太紧张了，”他说。

诺马克（NoMark）在 Instagram 上广为人知，他因发布自己戴着黑色面具并执行小型治安任务的视频而在网上获得了数十万粉丝：驱散酒吧外的打斗，闯入他认为“严重污染城市”的炼油厂。 《明尼苏达明星论坛报》称他为“明尼阿波利斯的蝙蝠侠”。 他在匿名的情况下接受了《卫报》的采访，讨论了潜在的非法行为。

在这个六月的夜晚，他把目光投向了一个新的目标：美国公司Flock Safety生产的自动车牌阅读器（ALPR）。

这些黑色摄像机连接到矩形太阳能电池板上，通常安装在杆子上，可以拍摄过往车辆的照片，并将这些照片与大型数据库进行比较。 它们引发了全国范围内支持隐私的批评者的强烈反对，他们指出公共记录表明这些设备可以帮助执法部门密切关注特定的车牌和驾驶这些汽车的人。 它们可以从公共场所的无辜行为中扫描出如此多的人的位置——无论目标是否是犯罪嫌疑人，而且没有搜查令——这导致了人们对大规模监控的担忧。

Flock 总部位于佐治亚州，估值 84 亿美元，该公司表示，其摄像头每月在美国几乎每个州的约 6,000 个社区扫描车牌数十亿次。

该公司在 2 月份的一篇博文中表示，其 ALPR“不是大规模监控工具”，并且“无法跟踪车辆，更不用说个人了”。

在塔可钟街对面，NoMark 不停地思考自己是否会被抓到，肾上腺素飙升，让人感到麻痹——尽管这对他的网络形象来说是“符合品牌形象的”，这为他在 Instagram 和 TikTok 上赢得了超过 70 万粉丝。 几分钟后，在路上没有发现任何汽车，他爬上杆子几英尺，用胶带粘住相机以挡住镜头，并剪断了为整个操作供电的电线。 随后他结束了手机录音并逃跑了。

如今，诺马克在这些远足中变得更加平静，在拆下十几台摄像机后，他只花了几分钟就完成了工作，他说。 但他仍然认为警方正在寻找他。 即使他确实被捕，他也希望指控不会太严厉——更重要的是，他“只是想传达一个信息”。

“如果我认为正确的话，我就不会害怕去做，”他说。 “这些事情在全国范围内发生得如此之快，以至于这是应对它们的唯一方法。”

明尼阿波利斯相机破坏者并不孤单。 随着人们对与 Flock 签订的执法合同越来越愤怒，全国各地的治安维护者开始自行动手，砸碎、阻碍或拆除这些摄像机。 许多人都在发挥自己的创意：对设备进行“油漆轰炸”，在损坏设备后在现场插上美国国旗，3D 打印物体来帮助遮挡摄像机的视线，并留下诸如“哈哈哈，你们这群监控者都被毁了”之类的彩色信息。 一些有影响力的人甚至利用公众对该公司的负面看法，伪造 Flock 的停止函。

《卫报》在 23 个州发现了至少 33 起破坏、破坏和毁坏 Flock 摄像机的事件，这些事件似乎带有抗议监控的明确信息。

弗洛克和美国各地的警察部门表示，这些摄像头对于公共安全来说是不可或缺的，它们可以捕捉有助于调查的车辆详细信息，例如车牌号码以及车辆的品牌和型号。 弗洛克的网站还宣传这些摄像头如何通过“可疑车辆经过时”向警察发出警报来“实时制止犯罪”，这表明警察可以根据这些线索迅速采取行动追捕目标。 该公司首席执行官加勒特·兰利 (Garrett Langley) 表示，一些支持隐私的批评者希望“使无法无天的行为正常化”并“削弱公共安全”。

NoMark 尚未因反对 Flock 摄像机的活动而被捕。 其他人则面临指控。 弗吉尼亚州萨福克市的杰弗里·索文 (Jeffrey Sovern) 因涉嫌损坏十几台 Flock 摄像机而被指控破坏财产。 索文尚未承认这一行为，但他告诉警方，他认为这些摄像头违反宪法。

他在为支付法律费用而创建的 GoFundMe 上写道：“我会看到一线希望，这可能成为一场更大的运动的催化剂，以减少侵入性监控。”

其他一些案件也受到刑事指控。 在新墨西哥州，杰文·马丁内斯 (Jevon Martinez) 因涉嫌毁坏 13 台 Flock 摄像机而被捕。

当被问及是否会“继续拆除这些 Flock 摄像机”时，马丁内斯告诉当地新闻电台 KRQE：“当然。 它们对公共安全构成明显且现实的威胁。” 该新闻媒体还报道称，其中一台受损的 Flock 摄像机附近有一个标牌，上面写着：“不客气，新墨西哥共和国。”

Flock 没有对治安维护者打碎其摄像头一事发表评论，但在 7 月中旬发表了一篇博文，内容是帮助政府机构在摄像头损坏时做出反应。

该公司写道：“我们已经为此做好了计划。”并补充说，保护计划可供购买。

执法部门意识到了这种强烈反对并做出了回应。 据记者 Dan Boguslaw 报道，数十个州融合中心——联邦和地方机构共享犯罪和恐怖主义情报的协作中心——今年夏天在执法机构之间分发了备忘录，指示官员监控反 Flock 的宣传，作为保护国家安全指令的一部分。 博古斯瓦夫从威斯康星州情报机构获得的一份报告呼吁在抗议活动和八月中旬的“全国行动周”等活动期间提高警惕和巡逻。 该情报摘要还建议当地执法部门向融合中心报告对 ALPR 的“破坏、破坏或破坏”行为。

羊群面临公众的反对

网上的同情之风并没有对弗洛克有利。 有关治安维持者案件的新闻文章和视频得到了网上评论者的支持，他们发布了捏造的、睦邻不在场的证据，比如在相机被毁时看到被告方营救狗或在施粥厨房提供食物。

反 Flock 在线生态系统还提供了针对摄像头的技巧和策略的交流。 一位 Reddit 发帖者分享了一个物体的 3D 打印文件，他说该物体可以帮助阻挡摄像头，而不会损坏摄像头或违反破坏法律。

明尼阿波利斯市的诺马克说，他每天都会收到数十条希望提供帮助的人发来的消息，让他知道他们正在采取类似的行动，或者寻求有关保持安全的建议。 他的回答含糊其辞，因为他不希望自己的言论导致人们被捕。 他告诉那些写信给他的人，要避免开车经过摄像头，并确保他们在深夜没有其他人在场的情况下出去。 他重申，他们应该完全遮盖起来，包括脸部和双手。

他还告诉他们：“永远遮住相机。”

明尼阿波利斯的蝙蝠侠认为，要实现变革，既需要对民选官员施加政治压力，也需要自卫行为。 他认为出席市议会会议（他曾多次不戴口罩出席会议）是有帮助的，但“这显然需要时间，而且并不总是有效”。

“你花的时间越多，他们获得的关于人们的数据就越多，”他说。

当治安维持者拆除摄像头时，隐私倡导者寻求政策改变

近年来，包括奥斯汀和丹佛在内的 80 多个城市已经解散、决定不续签或拒绝与 Flock 的合同，或者停用该公司的摄像头，尽管活动人士仍然担心这些设备在这些地区的继续使用。

除了普遍的监控蔓延之外，隐私倡导者还担心美国移民和海关执法局有能力通过法律漏洞获取这些摄像头信息来追捕移民。

警察也将摄像机用于个人目的。 一些人在滥用这些设备跟踪人们后失去了工作。 尽管车牌读取是摄像头的主要功能，但 404 Media 上周报道称，警方已使用 Flock 的搜索功能来寻找具有独特标记（例如纹身和特定 T 恤）的人，而不仅仅是汽车。

国会正在注意到这一点，本月早些时候，德克萨斯州的一名立法者提出了一项法案，要求对 Flock 摄像头收集的数据提供授权。

并非所有的反弗洛克行动都采取破坏相机的形式。 草根组织 DeFlock 创建的众包地图绘制了全国超过 115,000 个 ALPR。 该组织的网站还允许用户查看他们的车牌是否已在 Flock 系统中被搜索、获取避免 ALPR 的指示以及查找即将举行的有关市政 Flock 合同的会议。

Flock 的首席执行官也注意到了 DeFlock 的倡导，并将该组织描述为“恐怖主义”，但最近为该标签道歉。 在一条推文中，他将 DeFlock 的受欢迎程度归因于他的公司“对人们对 ALPR 的问题和担忧的回应不充分”。 该公司正在适应这种强烈反对，取消了一项始终开启的录音功能，即“人体遇险检测”，该功能旨在检测尖叫声。

DeFlock 位于弗吉尼亚州诺福克的当地分会表示，它不支持治安维持者针对 Flock 摄像头，但也不主张反对这种做法。

弗吉尼亚州分会正在努力确保该市取消或不再续签与弗洛克的合同，但到目前为止尚未取得成功，成员们对这一话题的发言限制感到特别愤怒。 据《弗吉尼亚飞行员报》报道，在上个月的市议会会议上，市长实施了一项减少重复评论的规定，以限制想要表达对弗洛克担忧的发言者数量。

DeFlock 发言人表示：“我们认识到，这是旨在阻止人们的声音被听到的系统的必然结果。”
